title: Complementing Self-Consistency with Cross-Model Disagreement for Uncertainty Quantification
one_liner: Measure uncertainty from two sources at once: variation within one model's repeated answers and disagreement across several similar-size models.
lead: A language model can be wrong while sounding certain. A common way to detect uncertainty is self-consistency: ask the same model several times and see whether its answers vary. That captures one kind of uncertainty, but it breaks when the model repeats the same wrong answer over and over. In that case the within-model spread is low even though the answer is unreliable. This paper studies that failure mode and adds a second signal: do several different models, each of similar scale, produce semantically different answers for the same prompt? The method calls the first signal aleatoric uncertainty, meaning variation inside one model's own answer samples, and the second signal epistemic uncertainty, meaning disagreement between models beyond what each model shows internally. Adding both gives a total uncertainty score that catches cases where one model is confidently wrong but peer models do not agree with it.

problem.h2: Why repeated sampling from one model can miss confident mistakes
paras: If a model answers a prompt five times and gives five different answers, we have direct evidence that the model is unsure. That is the intuition behind self-consistency as an uncertainty score.

The problem is the opposite case. A model can lock onto one wrong reasoning pattern and repeat it across samples. Then self-consistency reports low uncertainty because the samples agree, even though the answer is still wrong. Looking only inside one model misses the possibility that the model's whole belief state is miscalibrated.

callout.html: Keep the within-model variation score, but add a second score that asks whether other models disagree in meaning with that answer more than each model disagrees with itself.

panels.title: 1. One model answers five times
panels.caption: Repeated samples can all agree even when the answer is wrong.

panels.title: 2. Self-consistency looks low
panels.caption: Within one model, the answers appear stable, so the usual uncertainty score says little is wrong.

panels.title: 3. Other models answer differently
panels.caption: Across models, the answer meanings may diverge sharply.

panels.title: 4. Compare cross-model and within-model agreement
panels.caption: A large gap means one model's certainty is not shared by its peers.

panels.title: 5. Sum both uncertainty sources
panels.caption: Total uncertainty rises for confident failures that self-consistency alone would miss.

steps.b: Sample several answers from one model.
steps.text: Measure how much that model varies across repeated runs, because low internal variation is the standard self-consistency signal.

steps.b: Sample answers from a small peer ensemble.
steps.text: Use several models of similar size, because the method wants disagreement that reflects different learned beliefs rather than only huge scale differences.
Compare how similar the generated answers are in semantic content, because the method cares about whether answers mean the same thing rather than whether they share surface words.
Measure how much more the models disagree with each other than each model disagrees with itself, because that gap isolates uncertainty hidden by one model's repeated confidence.
Combine within-model spread and cross-model disagreement, because each captures a different reason an answer may be unreliable.

paras: The paper changes uncertainty estimation from a single-model self-consistency score into a two-part score that also uses disagreement across similar-size models.
object.object: the source of evidence used to judge whether a generated answer is trustworthy

hidden.name: disagreement that is invisible inside one model
paras: The key hidden quantity is not raw answer diversity. It is the extra disagreement that appears only when we compare several models to each other. If one model is consistently wrong in the same way, its internal samples will look stable. But if peer models answer with different meanings, that exposes uncertainty that self-consistency cannot see.

The paper estimates that hidden quantity by comparing inter-model similarity with intra-model similarity, where similarity means how close two generated answers are in meaning. A large gap says the models disagree with each other more than they disagree with themselves, so the answer should be treated cautiously even if one model sounds certain.

heat.caption: The darkest cells mark the information self-consistency misses: disagreement visible only across models.

reads.html: Ask not only whether one model repeats itself, but also whether its peers agree with the meaning of that answer.
Epistemic uncertainty is estimated as the gap between inter-model and intra-model sequence-level semantic similarity, then combined with self-consistency to form total uncertainty.

mechanism.h2: Why peer disagreement catches confident failures
paras: Self-consistency measures randomness inside one model's sampling process. That is useful when the model is wavering between several answers. It is not enough when the model has settled on one wrong answer pattern, because repeated samples then all support the same mistake.

Cross-model disagreement adds a second view. Different models trained on different data orders, initialization histories, or tuning decisions often make different errors. If one model is wrong but several peers give a different answer meaning, the disagreement reveals that the apparent certainty was local to that model rather than shared by the broader model family.

Comparing cross-model similarity against within-model similarity is the key step because it filters out cases where all models are naturally diverse on the prompt. The method does not flag every disagreement. It flags disagreement that is larger across models than within each model's own samples, which is the pattern expected when one model's confidence is not well founded.

stages.s: multiple answer samples from each model in a small peer set
take the excess cross-model disagreement and add it to self-consistency
uncertainty score that catches repeated wrong answers

math.words: Total uncertainty is the sum of the within-model uncertainty term and the cross-model disagreement term.
math.equation: total_uncertainty = aleatoric_uncertainty + epistemic_uncertainty, where epistemic_uncertainty = between_model_disagreement - within_model_disagreement
symbols: variation across repeated samples from one model
extra disagreement that appears across models beyond their own internal variation
how different the answer meanings are across models
how different the answer meanings are across samples from the same model

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose one model answers a prompt five times and the answers are nearly identical in meaning.
Now compare that answer to two peer models and find that their answers differ strongly in meaning.
The between-model disagreement is high while the within-model disagreement stays low.
The epistemic term becomes large, so the total uncertainty rises even though self-consistency alone would stay small.
That is exactly the pattern the method wants to catch.

math.note: The extra term is designed for black-box access, so it only needs generated text from each model rather than internal model states.

charts.title: Self-consistency only
charts.note: This view misses cases where one model repeats the same wrong answer, because low internal variation looks falsely reassuring.

charts.title: Self-consistency plus cross-model gap
charts.note: The gain comes from adding evidence that one model's certainty is not shared by peers, so risky answers rise in uncertainty even when repeated samples look stable.

items.b: The peer models can share the same blind spot.
items.html: If several models are wrong for the same reason and say nearly the same thing, cross-model disagreement stays low and the extra uncertainty term will not rescue the failure.

If the answer-meaning comparison says two answers are close when they are not, or far when they are close, the epistemic term will be distorted because it is built directly from those similarity values.

items.b: Very different model families may add irrelevant disagreement.
items.html: If the peer set mixes models with very different capabilities or styles, disagreement may reflect style differences rather than true answer uncertainty.
The method works best with a small, comparable peer set and a strong meaning-similarity scorer, because then the cross-model gap reflects genuine belief differences rather than formatting noise.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Pick a benchmark with long-form answers and known correctness labels. For each prompt, sample several answers from three similar-size models, compute self-consistency, compute the cross-model gap, and sort prompts by each uncertainty score. Then test two behaviors: ranking calibration and selective abstention. The demo should show that prompts flagged by the combined score contain more confident wrong answers than prompts flagged by self-consistency alone.
demo.closing: The key evidence is not just higher uncertainty on random errors, but higher uncertainty on the cases where one model sounds most certain and is still wrong.
